rag/corpus/terraform/state_backend_s3.tf.title: Terraform Remote State Backend — S3 + DynamoDB Locking

entries.concept: Terraform Remote State Backend — S3 + DynamoDB Locking
entries.what_it_does: Defines the production-standard Terraform remote state backend: an S3 bucket stores the terraform.tfstate file and a DynamoDB table provides state locking so two engineers or CI runs cannot apply simultaneously. The backend infrastructure is created once by a bootstrap configuration, after which state is migrated to the remote backend with `terraform init -migrate-state`. The S3 backend block (bucket, key, region, encrypt, dynamodb_table) is placed in backend.tf/versions.tf of every consuming module, not in main.tf.
when_to_use: Use for any Terraform managed by more than one engineer or by CI/CD — local state does not support locking or sharing
Run the bootstrap configuration ONCE to create the bucket and lock table, then migrate state to the remote backend

Use a per-workspace state key of the form `${var.environment}/${var.component}/terraform.tfstate` (e.g. prod/vpc/terraform.tfstate, staging/rds/terraform.tfstate) to isolate state per environment and component
best_practices: Enable S3 bucket versioning so any previous state file can be restored after a bad apply
Set `prevent_destroy = true` on both the state bucket and the lock table so `terraform destroy` cannot delete them accidentally
Use DynamoDB billing_mode PAY_PER_REQUEST with a single LockID (String) hash key — no capacity planning required for the lock table
Keep the backend block in backend.tf or versions.tf (not main.tf) and pin the AWS provider (~> 5.0) and required_version (>= 1.5.0)
security_considerations: Enable server-side encryption on the state bucket (AES256, or a KMS key ARN for stricter control) — state files contain resource attributes and sometimes secrets
Block ALL public access on the state bucket (block_public_acls, block_public_policy, ignore_public_acls, restrict_public_buckets) — state must never be public

Grant the CI/CD role a least-privilege IAM policy scoped to exactly the state bucket (s3:GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject/ListBucket) and the lock table (dynamodb:GetItem/PutItem/DeleteItem/DescribeTable) — not account-wide S3 or DynamoDB access
entries.code_reference: terraform { backend "s3" { bucket=..., key="${env}/${component}/terraform.tfstate", region=..., encrypt=true, dynamodb_table="terraform-state-locks" } } plus aws_s3_bucket (versioning + SSE + public_access_block + prevent_destroy) and aws_dynamodb_table (PAY_PER_REQUEST, LockID hash key, prevent_destroy).

rag/corpus/terraform/aws_iam_roles.tf.title: Terraform AWS IAM Roles & Policies — Production Patterns

entries.concept: EC2 Instance IAM Role — SSM Access and Scoped S3 Read
entries.what_it_does: Creates an IAM role assumable by the EC2 service, exposed to instances through an aws_iam_instance_profile. The role attaches the AWS-managed AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy (enabling Systems Manager Session Manager) and a custom inline-built policy granting s3:GetObject and s3:ListBucket on a single named application bucket.
when_to_use: Use to give an EC2 workload read access to one specific S3 bucket without embedding long-lived credentials on the instance
Use the SSM managed policy to enable Session Manager so administrators do not need SSH (port 22) open to the instance
best_practices: Attach permissions to EC2 via an instance profile, not by placing access keys on the host
Prefer SSM Session Manager over opening port 22 for shell access — it replaces SSH and leaves an auditable trail
Namespace roles with a path (e.g. /app/) and tag them (Environment, ManagedBy=terraform) for organization and cleanup
security_considerations: Scope the S3 policy to the explicit bucket ARN and its objects (arn:aws:s3:::<bucket> and /*) rather than Resource: "*" — this is least privilege
Grant only the actions the workload needs (read-only GetObject/ListBucket here), not s3:*
entries.code_reference: aws_iam_role ec2_app (assume_role_policy Principal Service=ec2.amazonaws.com) + aws_iam_instance_profile + aws_iam_role_policy_attachment to AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore + aws_iam_policy ec2_s3_read (s3:GetObject/ListBucket scoped to var.app_bucket_name).

entries.concept: CI/CD IAM Role via GitHub Actions OIDC — No Static Keys
entries.what_it_does: Creates an IAM role that GitHub Actions assumes through OIDC federation using sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity against the token.actions.githubusercontent.com OIDC provider. Trust is constrained by a StringLike condition on the token `sub` (repo:my-org/my-repo:*) and a StringEquals condition on `aud` (sts.amazonaws.com). The attached policy grants ECR push/pull actions scoped to the environment's repository path.
when_to_use: Use for CI/CD pipelines that deploy to AWS so the pipeline authenticates via short-lived OIDC tokens instead of long-lived IAM user access keys
Use when the pipeline must push container images to ECR and pull them back during deploy
best_practices: Prefer OIDC web-identity federation over storing static AWS access keys in CI secrets — there are no long-lived credentials to rotate or leak

Scope the ECR object actions (BatchCheckLayerAvailability, PutImage, UploadLayerPart, BatchGetImage, GetDownloadUrlForLayer, etc.) to the specific repository ARN path (repository/${var.environment}/*)
security_considerations: Restrict the trust policy `sub` to your exact org/repo (repo:my-org/my-repo:*) — never use "*", which would let any GitHub repo assume the role
ecr:GetAuthorizationToken requires Resource "*" by API design; keep all other ECR actions scoped to the repository path so a token leak cannot reach unrelated repositories
entries.code_reference: data.aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github + aws_iam_role github_actions_deploy (AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, StringLike sub, StringEquals aud) + aws_iam_policy github_actions_ecr (GetAuthorizationToken on *, other ECR actions scoped to repository/${env}/*).

entries.concept: EKS Worker Node IAM Role — Required Managed Policies
entries.what_it_does: Creates an IAM role assumable by the EC2 service for EKS worker nodes and attaches the three AWS-managed policies EKS nodes require: AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy (node registration), AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy (VPC CNI pod networking), and AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly (pull images from ECR).
when_to_use: Use as the instance role for EKS managed or self-managed worker nodes that must join the cluster, run the VPC CNI, and pull images from ECR
best_practices: Attach exactly the three required managed policies (worker node, CNI, ECR read-only) — these are the documented minimum for nodes to function
security_considerations: Permissions on the node role apply to every pod scheduled on the node; use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) to grant application-specific AWS permissions at the pod level instead of broadening this node role
entries.code_reference: aws_iam_role eks_node (assume by ec2.amazonaws.com) + role_policy_attachments to AmazonEKSWorkerNodePolicy, AmazonEKS_CNI_Policy, AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly.

entries.concept: Production VPC Layout — Multi-AZ Public/Private Subnets with Per-AZ NAT
entries.what_it_does: Provisions a production VPC with DNS support and hostnames enabled, an Internet Gateway, and one public and one private subnet per availability zone (CIDRs derived deterministically via cidrsubnet). Public subnets set map_public_ip_on_launch=true and route 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway; private subnets have no public IPs and route 0.0.0.0/0 to a per-AZ NAT Gateway (each with its own Elastic IP). The AZ list, VPC CIDR (default 10.0.0.0/16), region, and environment are variables.
when_to_use: Use as the network foundation for multi-AZ production workloads that need public ingress/egress (load balancers, NAT) and private application/data tiers
Use the availability_zones list variable to control how many AZs (and therefore subnets and NAT gateways) are created
best_practices: Derive subnet CIDRs with cidrsubnet(var.vpc_cidr, 8, index) so subnets are non-overlapping and deterministic across AZs
Deploy one NAT Gateway (and one Elastic IP) per AZ so a single AZ failure does not cut outbound access for the other AZs; associate each private subnet with its own per-AZ private route table
Enable enable_dns_support and enable_dns_hostnames on the VPC, and tag every resource with Environment, Tier (public/private), and ManagedBy=terraform
security_considerations: Keep map_public_ip_on_launch=false on private subnets so application and data tiers never receive public IPs
Place only internet-facing resources in public subnets; private subnets reach the internet only outbound through NAT, with no inbound path from the IGW
entries.code_reference: aws_vpc (DNS on) + aws_internet_gateway + aws_subnet.public/private (count over AZs, cidrsubnet) + aws_eip.nat + aws_nat_gateway (per AZ, depends_on IGW) + aws_route_table public(IGW)/private(NAT) + associations.

entries.what_it_does: Enables VPC Flow Logs capturing ALL traffic for the VPC and delivering them to a dedicated CloudWatch Log Group (retention 30 days). A dedicated IAM role assumable by vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com grants the logs:CreateLogGroup/CreateLogStream/PutLogEvents/DescribeLogGroups/DescribeLogStreams actions needed to write the logs.
when_to_use: Use as a security and network-observability baseline so VPC traffic (accepted and rejected) is recorded for audit, troubleshooting, and threat detection
best_practices: Capture traffic_type ALL (not just ACCEPT or REJECT) for complete visibility
Set an explicit CloudWatch log retention (30 days here) so logs are kept long enough to investigate without growing unbounded
Use a dedicated flow-log IAM role rather than reusing an unrelated role
security_considerations: Flow logs provide the network-visibility signal needed to detect and scope intrusions and misconfigurations
The flow-log role's logs policy uses Resource "*"; tightening it to the specific log group ARN would further enforce least privilege
entries.code_reference: aws_flow_log (traffic_type ALL → CloudWatch) + aws_cloudwatch_log_group (/aws/vpc-flow-log/${env}, retention 30) + aws_iam_role flow_log (assume by vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com) + aws_iam_role_policy (logs:* actions, Resource "*").
